topic.ru: Три текста: что на самом деле называют опустыниванием, как лифт перевернул устройство города и спор о бесплатном общественном транспорте.

textTitles: Going up: the lift and the modern city

paragraphs.text: The word desertification suggests an image that is misleading in almost every respect. It calls to mind dunes advancing across fields and villages, a moving front that could in principle be halted by a wall of trees. What the term actually describes is the degradation of land in dry regions, a loss of the soil’s capacity to support plants that can happen anywhere within those regions, often in patches far from any existing desert. The land does not become a sea of sand; it becomes poorer, more easily eroded and less able to recover after a drought, and the change is frequently invisible until a bad year exposes it. It is as much a problem of poverty as of ecology, since the people most affected have the fewest alternatives.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Dry regions have always been variable, and this makes the problem unusually difficult to measure. Rainfall in a semi-arid area can vary by half from one year to the next, and vegetation responds quickly, so that a landscape that looks bare after two poor seasons may be green again after one good one. For decades, estimates of how fast the world’s drylands were deteriorating were based on observations made during droughts, and several of the most alarming figures turned out to describe temporary conditions rather than lasting damage. Separating a trend from a fluctuation requires records long enough to include several wet and dry periods.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Satellite images eventually provided such records, and they complicated the picture considerably. In some areas that had been described as advancing deserts, the long-term record showed vegetation recovering once rainfall returned to earlier levels, a pattern researchers now call greening. In others, the ground cover recovered in quantity but not in kind: perennial grasses with deep roots were replaced by annual plants and shrubs that are less useful to grazing animals and protect the soil less well. A green image, in other words, is not necessarily a healthy one, and the satellite shows the amount of plant material far more reliably than its type.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The causes are a combination of climate and land use, and their relative importance is disputed. Overgrazing, the cultivation of land that is too dry to farm reliably, and the removal of trees for fuel all reduce the plant cover that holds soil in place, while repeated droughts remove the reserves that would allow the land to recover. Early accounts tended to blame local farmers and herders almost entirely, and the policies that followed often restricted their movements. More recent work gives greater weight to rainfall and to economic pressures from outside, such as prices that encourage the expansion of crops into marginal land. Neither explanation, on its own, fits every region.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Mobile herding, once treated as part of the problem, is now often considered part of the solution. Herders who move their animals across large areas follow the rain and leave pastures to recover, and their practices evolved precisely to cope with unpredictable conditions. When herders were settled around permanent water points, as happened under several development programmes, the land near the wells was grazed bare while distant pastures went unused. Several countries have since changed their laws to protect traditional routes, although conflicts with farmers whose fields now cross those routes remain common. In one well-documented case, pastures that had been described as ruined recovered within three seasons once animals were again allowed to move between them.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Restoration has had mixed results, and the most expensive methods have not always been the most successful. Large tree-planting schemes intended to create green barriers have suffered high losses where species unsuited to the local conditions were chosen, or where the trees consumed groundwater that other plants needed. Cheaper techniques have sometimes worked better: farmers in parts of West Africa have protected the stumps and roots of trees that sprout naturally in their fields, and over two decades this practice has restored tree cover across several million hectares without any planting at all.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Simple structures that slow the movement of water have also proved effective. Lines of stones laid along the contours of a slope, half-moon-shaped pits dug to collect runoff, and small earth banks around fields all hold rain where it falls long enough for it to soak into the ground. The techniques are old, and some were revived by agricultural projects after being abandoned for a generation or more. Their value lies in the fact that farmers can build and maintain them without machinery, and that the benefit, a better harvest in a dry year, is visible to the people who did the work.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: None of this means that the threat has been exaggerated. Drylands support a large share of the world’s population, and a warming climate is expected to make droughts more frequent in several of them. What has changed is the understanding of where action is most useful. The image of a desert that must be stopped at its edge has given way to one of land that must be managed across its whole extent, by the people who live on it, in ways that allow it to recover between the bad years that will certainly come. Measuring success will require the same patience as measuring the problem did: long records, taken across good years and bad, rather than snapshots taken in a crisis.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Going up: the lift and the modern city

paragraphs.text: Before the middle of the nineteenth century, the height of a building was limited less by what could be built than by what people were willing to climb. Offices and apartments above the fifth or sixth floor were difficult to let, and the upper floors of tall buildings were often the cheapest, given to servants, storage or the poor. The most valuable space in any building was on the ground and first floors, where customers and residents could reach it without effort. That ordering of value, which had held for centuries, was reversed within a few decades by a machine that most people now use without thinking about it.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Hoisting platforms had existed for a long time, raised by ropes and powered by people, animals, water or steam. They were used for goods in mines, warehouses and factories, and passengers were generally kept off them for a simple reason: if the rope broke, the platform fell. The decisive invention was therefore not a way of lifting but a way of not falling. In the 1850s an American mechanic demonstrated a safety device in which a spring, released the moment the rope went slack, pushed metal teeth into notched rails on either side of the shaft, locking the platform in place. Earlier safety mechanisms had been proposed, but none had been shown convincingly enough to persuade the public.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The demonstration was theatrical by design. The inventor stood on a raised platform in front of a crowd, ordered the rope to be cut, and remained exactly where he was. Public confidence was the obstacle the device had to overcome, and the performance was aimed at it as much as at engineers. Within a few years passenger lifts were being installed in department stores and hotels, where they served partly as attractions in their own right, and building owners began to discover that upper floors reached by a lift could be let at prices close to those of the lower ones.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The technology developed in stages over the following decades. Steam-driven lifts were replaced by hydraulic ones, in which water under pressure pushed a piston that raised the car; these were smooth and reliable but required a shaft beneath the building as deep as the building was tall, which set a practical limit on height. Electric lifts, which appeared in the 1880s, removed that limit, since the car was pulled from above by a cable wound around a motor-driven drum. The later introduction of counterweights, which balanced the weight of the car, reduced the energy needed and allowed much faster travel. Each stage made the car faster, quieter and cheaper to run.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: With the lift in place, the economics of the tall building were transformed. Steel frames made it possible to build higher than walls of brick or stone could support, but without the lift that height would have been worthless, because no one would have paid to occupy it. Together the two technologies made land in city centres dramatically more productive, since a single plot could now hold dozens of floors of offices. Land prices in the business districts of the fastest-growing cities rose accordingly, which in turn made building upwards the only way of making such expensive land pay. The two inventions are usually celebrated separately, but neither would have transformed the city alone.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The social geography of the building was turned upside down. The top floors, once the least desirable, became the most prestigious, commanding the best views, the most light and the least noise from the street. Penthouse apartments and executive offices moved to the summit, while the ground floor was given to shops and lobbies. Some historians argue that this reversal did more than any other change to make height a symbol of status, and that the preference for living and working high above the street, now taken for granted in many cities, is only about a century and a half old. Before the lift, the equivalent address would have been the attic.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The lift also imposed limits of its own. In a very tall building, lift shafts occupy a large share of each floor, since enough cars must be provided to carry everyone at the busiest times of day, and above a certain height the space consumed by shafts makes additional floors uneconomic. Engineers have responded with express lifts that stop only at certain levels, with cars stacked two to a shaft, and with sky lobbies where passengers change from one lift to another. Some recent systems use lighter cables made of carbon fibre, which allow a single car to travel further before the weight of the cable becomes a problem.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The lift is so reliable today that its safety is rarely considered, though it is one of the most heavily used forms of transport in the world, carrying more passengers every day in some cities than the buses and trains combined. What the history suggests is that the most important feature of the machine was never its capacity to lift but the confidence it gave people to use it. The skyline of every modern city depends, in the end, on a spring and a set of metal teeth that most passengers have never seen and would not recognise.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: A number of towns and cities have abolished fares on their buses and trams, and several more are considering it. The idea has an obvious appeal: public transport becomes as easy to use as a pavement, the cost of collecting fares disappears, and people who cannot afford a ticket are no longer excluded from jobs and services. Yet the experience of the places that have tried it is more varied than either supporters or critics tend to admit, and the question of whether fare-free transport works depends heavily on what it is expected to achieve. The debate is also shaped by who pays: fares fall on passengers, while the replacement money usually comes from all taxpayers, including those who never use the service.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Elena Varga, a transport economist, notes that fares usually cover only part of the cost of running a network, often between a third and a half, and that in some smaller systems the cost of selling and checking tickets consumes a large share of what the fares bring in. For such systems, she argues, abolishing fares loses less money than the headline figures suggest. For large networks where fares pay for a substantial part of operations, the calculation is quite different, and the lost income must be replaced from taxes or the service will decline. Where ticket machines, inspectors and fare-collection software are expensive to maintain, the saving can be substantial.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The most consistent finding is that free travel increases the number of passengers. The difficulty lies in where the new passengers come from. Jonas Ekberg, who has studied several fare-free schemes, found that a large proportion of the additional trips were made by people who would otherwise have walked or cycled, and a smaller proportion by people who would otherwise have driven. A policy intended to reduce car traffic may therefore succeed in filling buses while leaving the roads almost as congested as before, and he regards this as the central weakness of free travel as an environmental measure. Car use in the towns he studied fell only slightly.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Supporters reply that the environmental case was never the strongest one. Amara Nwosu, who works on social policy, argues that the main benefit is access: people on low incomes, the young and the unemployed can reach work, training and public services without calculating whether each trip is worth the fare. In her studies of towns that removed fares, residents of poorer districts made more trips to the town centre and reported fewer occasions on which they had stayed at home because of the cost. She describes free transport as a public service in the same category as street lighting, whose value is not measured by how many people it takes out of cars.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Quality is a further concern. Transport operators and some passengers’ groups fear that a network which earns nothing from its users will be the first to suffer when public budgets are cut, and that crowding will increase as passenger numbers grow without additional vehicles. Rafael Soto, who advises regional authorities, argues that for most people frequency and reliability matter more than price, and that the same money spent on more services would attract more drivers than the removal of fares. He does not oppose free travel as such, but insists that it should come only after the service is good enough to be worth using. Crowding, in his experience, discourages new passengers faster than a fare does.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Much depends on the details of each scheme. Some cities have made travel free only for residents, others only for particular groups such as students or older people, and still others only at certain times of day. Targeted schemes cost less and can be directed at the people who benefit most, but they bring back some of the administration that universal free travel removes, since eligibility must be checked. A few cities have combined free transport with charges for driving into the centre, which addresses both sides of the choice between car and bus at once.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The evidence so far is limited in one important respect. Most of the places that have abolished fares are small or medium-sized, with modest networks and relatively low fare income, and it is not clear that their experience would apply to a large metropolitan system. Nor have most schemes been running long enough to show whether the changes in behaviour they produce are permanent. Studies that follow passengers over many years, rather than comparing the first year after the change with the year before, are still rare, and without them the long-term effects remain a matter of informed guesswork.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The fair conclusion is that free public transport is a tool rather than a solution. It is a good one for widening access in places where fares are a significant barrier and where the lost income is manageable, and a weak one for reducing traffic unless it is combined with measures that make driving less attractive. Whether a city should adopt it depends on which of those problems it is trying to solve, and on whether it is prepared to pay for the service that free travel will need. A city that asks the tool to do something it was not designed for should not be surprised when it disappoints.
paragraphs.label: H
